about: The politics pack (US midterms on 3 November 2026): hand-curated items in five categories, each with a `tier` (1 = famous names and years, 2 = events and money, 3 = procedure and detail). pol_elected: the year a member of Congress who sits in October 2026 (checked on congress.gov on 2026-10-05) first won election to the chamber in the name; the election year, not the swearing-in; special elections and runoffs count; party and state in `note`; `famous: false` when the member's English Wikipedia article averaged under 50,000 user views a month in July-September 2026. pol_timeline: US federal political events from October 1996 to October 2026 at month precision (`month`, YYYY-MM): laws signed, shutdowns begun and ended, impeachment votes, Speaker elections, Supreme Court decisions, changes of party control. pol_numbers: integers with a `unit` (electoral votes, House seats, yea votes, popular votes, years old, years). pol_money: dated dollar figures from FEC filings (fec.gov) or CBO estimates (cbo.gov), `volatile: true` with `as_of` (YYYY-MM), the date in the name; never in ranked rounds. pol_drama: documented public events (expulsions, censures, reprimands, committee removals, resignations, indictments, pleas and verdicts with their outcome, ethics findings, floor moments) at month precision, sourced to a chamber, a court or another official record, or to two major news organisations named in `note`; nothing about private life, health or family, and no unproven allegations; `famous` only when the subject's article averaged 50,000+ user views a month in July-September 2026; `fun` states a plain fact from the sources named in `note`. Names in pol_timeline and pol_drama carry no date. Each value was checked against its source's text on 2026-10-05 (`fact_checked`); the text fragment in `source` marks the passage, and `note` gives the exact day and the publisher. Method, counts and exclusions: analysis/items_pipeline/POLITICS_NOTES.md.

items.name: The House expels George Santos
items.note: Republican, New York; 1 December 2023, H. Res. 878, 311-114 with 2 present (Office of the Historian, U.S. House)
items.fun: The vote was 311-114. He was the sixth member ever expelled from the House, and the first since 2002.

items.name: George Santos pleads guilty to wire fraud and identity theft
items.note: Republican, New York; 19 August 2024, federal court in Central Islip (U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York)
items.fun: He admitted filing false FEC reports, stealing identities and charging credit cards without authorization.

items.name: George Santos is sentenced to 87 months in prison
items.note: Republican, New York; sentenced 25 April 2025 (U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York); sentence commuted 17 October 2025 (Office of the Pardon Attorney)
items.fun: President Trump commuted the sentence on 17 October 2025.

items.name: The House censures Paul Gosar
items.note: Republican, Arizona; 17 November 2021, H. Res. 789, 223-207 (Office of the Historian, U.S. House)
items.fun: The vote was 223-207. It was the first House censure since Charles Rangel's in 2010.

items.name: The House reprimands Joe Wilson for interrupting Obama's speech to Congress
items.note: Republican, South Carolina; 15 September 2009, H. Res. 744, 240-179 (Office of the Historian, U.S. House)
items.fun: The House voted 240-179 that interrupting the President's remarks was a breach of decorum.

items.name: The House reprimands David Schweikert
items.note: Republican, Arizona; 31 July 2020, H. Res. 1074, by voice vote (Office of the Historian, U.S. House)
items.fun: The reprimand passed by voice vote. It cited campaign finance violations and misuse of his office budget.

items.name: The House reprimands Speaker Newt Gingrich
items.note: Republican, Georgia, then Speaker; 21 January 1997, H. Res. 31, 395-28 (Office of the Historian, U.S. House); "House Reprimands, Penalizes Speaker" (The Washington Post, 22 January 1997, cited by Wikipedia)
items.fun: The vote was 395-28. The case cited a tax-exempt group used for political purposes and inaccurate answers to the Ethics Committee.

items.name: The House removes Marjorie Taylor Greene from her committees
items.note: Republican, Georgia; 4 February 2021, H. Res. 72, roll call 25, 230-199 (Congress.gov; Clerk of the House)
items.fun: The vote was 230-199, with 11 Republicans voting yes. She lost her seats on the Budget and Education committees.

items.name: The House rejects white supremacy after remarks by Steve King
items.note: Republican, Iowa; 15 January 2019, H. Res. 41, roll call 32, 424-1; the resolution quotes his remarks of 10 January 2019 (Congress.gov; Clerk of the House)
items.fun: The resolution passed 424-1. The one no vote came from a Democrat.

items.name: Jim Jordan loses a third House vote for Speaker
items.note: Republican, Ohio; 20 October 2023, roll call 525, after ballots on 17 and 18 October, rolls 521 and 523 (Clerk of the House)
items.fun: Hakeem Jeffries got 210 votes and Jordan 194, while 25 votes went to eight other Republicans.

items.name: John McCain votes no as the Senate rejects a health care repeal amendment
items.note: Republican, Arizona; 28 July 2017, vote 179, on an amendment to the American Health Care Act of 2017 (U.S. Senate)
items.fun: It failed 49-51. Three Republicans voted no: Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and John McCain.

items.name: Ted Cruz speaks for 21 hours against the Affordable Care Act
items.note: Republican, Texas; 24-25 September 2013, during the debate on the 2014 continuing resolution (U.S. Senate Historical Office)
items.fun: He spoke for 21 hours and 19 minutes. The all-night session ran 34 hours and 11 minutes.

items.name: Arlen Specter switches from Republican to Democrat
items.note: Republican until the switch, Pennsylvania; became a Democrat on 30 April 2009 (U.S. Senate)
items.fun: He had been elected as a Republican five times, in 1980, 1986, 1992, 1998 and 2004.

items.name: Duncan Hunter pleads guilty to stealing campaign funds
items.note: Republican, California; 3 December 2019 (U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of California)
items.fun: The plea covered more than $150,000 in campaign money spent on personal use from 2010 to 2016.

items.name: Chris Collins pleads guilty in an insider trading case
items.note: Republican, New York; 1 October 2019 (U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York)
items.fun: He had resigned his seat in Congress the day before, on 30 September 2019.

items.name: A jury convicts Jeff Fortenberry of lying to federal investigators
items.note: Republican, Nebraska; 24 March 2022 (U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California); reversed 26 December 2023 (U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit)
items.fun: An appeals court reversed the conviction in December 2023, saying the trial was held in the wrong venue.

items.name: Michael Grimm pleads guilty to tax fraud
items.note: Republican, New York; 23 December 2014 (U.S. Department of Justice)
items.fun: He admitted hiding over $900,000 in restaurant receipts and lying under oath while in Congress.

items.name: A jury convicts Steve Stockman of fraud and money laundering
items.note: Republican, Texas, former member; 12 April 2018 (U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas)
items.fun: The counts included seven of mail and wire fraud and 11 of money laundering.

items.name: Bob Ney pleads guilty to corruption charges
items.note: Republican, Ohio; 13 October 2006 (U.S. Department of Justice, sentencing release of 19 January 2007)
items.fun: He was sentenced to 30 months in prison in January 2007.

items.name: The Justice Department drops its case against Ted Stevens
items.note: Republican, Alaska; 1 April 2009, statement of Attorney General Eric Holder (U.S. Department of Justice)
items.fun: Attorney General Eric Holder chose to dismiss the indictment rather than hold a new trial.

items.name: Marjorie Taylor Greene resigns from the House
items.note: Republican, Georgia; 5 January 2026 (Clerk of the House); successor sworn in 14 April 2026 (Clerk of the House member data)
items.fun: Her seat stayed empty until Clay Fuller was sworn in on 14 April 2026.

items.name: House Republicans remove Liz Cheney from their leadership
items.note: Republican, Wyoming; 12 May 2021, by voice vote in a closed-door meeting (CBS News; NPR)
items.fun: She was removed as conference chair by voice vote, so there was no tally.

items.name: The House expels James Traficant
items.note: Democrat, Ohio; 24 July 2002, H. Res. 495, 420-1 with 9 present (Office of the Historian, U.S. House)
items.fun: The vote was 420-1. He had been convicted of charges including bribery conspiracy and racketeering.

items.name: The House censures Charles Rangel
items.note: Democrat, New York; 2 December 2010, H. Res. 1737, 333-79 (Office of the Historian, U.S. House)
items.fun: The vote was 333-79. The charges included using House letterhead to raise money.

items.name: The House censures Adam Schiff
items.note: Democrat, California; 21 June 2023, H. Res. 521, 213-209 with 6 present (Office of the Historian, U.S. House)
items.fun: The vote was 213-209, with 6 members voting present.

items.name: The House censures Rashida Tlaib
items.note: Democrat, Michigan; 7 November 2023, H. Res. 845, 234-188 with 4 present (Office of the Historian, U.S. House)
items.fun: The vote was 234-188, with 4 members voting present.

items.name: The House censures Jamaal Bowman over a building evacuation
items.note: Democrat, New York; 7 December 2023, H. Res. 914, 214-191 with 5 present (Office of the Historian, U.S. House)
items.fun: It passed 214-191. The resolution said he forced the evacuation of a House office building during a vote.

items.name: The House censures Al Green for disrupting Trump's address to Congress
items.note: Democrat, Texas; 6 March 2025, H. Res. 189, 224-198 with 2 present (Office of the Historian, U.S. House)
items.fun: The vote was 224-198. The resolution said he disrupted the President's joint address to Congress.

items.name: The House reprimands Laura Richardson
items.note: Democrat, California; 2 August 2012, H. Res. 755, by unanimous consent (Office of the Historian, U.S. House)
items.fun: The reprimand passed by unanimous consent. It was about House staff made to work on her campaign.

items.name: The House removes Ilhan Omar from the Foreign Affairs Committee
items.note: Democrat, Minnesota; 2 February 2023, H. Res. 76, roll call 105, 218-211 (Congress.gov; Clerk of the House)
items.fun: The vote was 218-211, along party lines, with one member voting present.

items.name: A jury convicts Bob Menendez of corruption
items.note: Democrat, New Jersey; 16 July 2024 (U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York)
items.fun: He was a sitting senator when the jury convicted him.

items.name: Bob Menendez is sentenced to 11 years in prison
items.note: Democrat, New Jersey; 29 January 2025 (U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York)
items.fun: Two businessmen in the same case got more than eight years and seven years.

items.name: The Senate Ethics Committee admonishes Bob Menendez
items.note: Democrat, New Jersey; 26 April 2018, public letter of admonition (Senate Select Committee on Ethics)
items.fun: The committee found he accepted gifts of significant value from Dr. Salomon Melgen for six years without approval.

items.name: The Senate Ethics Committee admonishes Robert Torricelli
items.note: Democrat, New Jersey; 30 July 2002, letter of admonition (Senate Select Committee on Ethics)
items.fun: The committee told him to pay the full retail value of a TV and a CD player he had accepted.

items.name: A jury convicts William Jefferson of bribery
items.note: Democrat, Louisiana; 5 August 2009 (U.S. Department of Justice)
items.fun: The jury found him guilty on 11 counts, including solicitation of bribes, money laundering and racketeering.

items.name: A jury convicts Chaka Fattah of racketeering conspiracy
items.note: Democrat, Pennsylvania; 21 June 2016 (U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania)
items.fun: The jury found him guilty of all charges against him.

items.name: Jesse Jackson Jr. pleads guilty to misusing campaign money
items.note: Democrat, Illinois; 20 February 2013 (U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia)
items.fun: He admitted that about $750,000 in campaign funds paid for personal items.

items.name: Henry Cuellar is charged with bribery
items.note: Democrat, Texas; indictment unsealed 3 May 2024 (U.S. Department of Justice); pardoned 2 December 2025 (Office of the Pardon Attorney)
items.fun: President Trump pardoned him on 2 December 2025. He had not been sentenced.

items.name: Corrine Brown pleads guilty to obstructing tax laws
items.note: Democrat, Florida, former member; 19 May 2022 (U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida)
items.fun: A jury had convicted her earlier, but that conviction was vacated on appeal.

items.name: Kyrsten Sinema leaves the Democratic Party
items.note: Democrat until the switch, Arizona; announced 9 December 2022, effective 3 January 2023 (U.S. Senate)
items.fun: The change took effect on 3 January 2023, at the start of the new Congress.

items.name: Joe Manchin leaves the Democratic Party
items.note: Democrat until the switch, West Virginia; 5 June 2024 (U.S. Senate)
items.fun: He kept caucusing with the Democrats after the switch.

items.name: Cory Booker gives the longest speech in Senate history
items.note: Democrat, New Jersey; April 2025 (U.S. Senate)
items.fun: He spoke for 25 hours and 5 minutes, passing Strom Thurmond's 24 hours and 18 minutes from 1957.

items.name: Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick resigns from the House
items.note: Democrat, Florida; 21 April 2026 (Clerk of the House); the Ethics Committee's sanctions hearing was set for that day, after a panel found 25 of 27 counts proven (House Committee on Ethics)
items.fun: She quit on the day of an Ethics sanctions hearing, after a panel found 25 of 27 counts against her proven.

items.name: Nancy Pelosi tears up Trump's State of the Union speech
items.note: Democrat, California, then Speaker; 4 February 2020 (NBC News; CBS News)
items.fun: She tore her copy in half right after he finished, while standing behind him.
